sections.html:
In Greenfield you can list with an agent, sell privately, or let a cash buyer purchase the house exactly as it stands. The city is in Milwaukee County, with 37,159 residents as of July 1, 2025, compared with 37,803 in the 2020 census.

An agent listing pays off for an updated home if you can tolerate weeks of tours. A direct sale is a better match for a worn kitchen, put-off repairs, an empty house or an estate. Either way, the paperwork ends at the Milwaukee County Register of Deeds with identical fee and return.

About 54.8 percent of households own, and the citywide value below is only a midpoint. An older house with original systems and finishes will probably sell for less.

Residents aged 65 and older total 21.9 percent, and the commute averages 22.2 minutes.

People rarely leave Greenfield once they buy. Nearly 89.2 percent of residents had not moved in the past year, and 37.6 percent of households are single people living alone, so you will often meet original kitchens, baths and mechanical systems. Of 18,035 housing units, 3.8 percent are vacant, and only 0.9 percent of owned homes sit empty.

Cold, wet winters put the roof, sump pump and furnace under a buyer's microscope. Keep receipts for recent service close at hand, and show them at the first tour or the first call with a direct buyer.

sections.h2: Checks with the city before listing
sections.html:
Phone the City of Greenfield building inspection office first. Ask about any permit left open, and about final inspections for an addition, a finished basement or a deck. A loose end like that tends to turn up during a buyer's file review and can stall a standard sale. Direct buyers often accept the file as is, yet you will want the facts.

  • Open building, electrical or plumbing permits.
  • Exterior orders from the city, for instance on a fence or accessory building.
  • Street or utility special assessments on the tax bill.
  • Tenant occupancy and lease terms.

If you plan fixes before selling, that office can also tell you which ones require a permit.

For a Greenfield house, the deed goes to the Milwaukee County Register of Deeds in downtown Milwaukee (901 N. 9th Street, Room 103). It keeps weekday hours of 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., indexes what you file and takes the transfer tax. The tax lands on the seller at 30 cents per $100 of value or fraction thereof, as Wis. Stat. 77.22.

Four stages cover most Greenfield closings:

  • Start title work and request a payoff letter from your lender.
  • Submit the electronic transfer return to the Wisconsin Department of Revenue.
  • Take the deed to the Register of Deeds for recording.
  • Get paid once liens and prorated taxes are cleared.

The list of exempt transfers includes inheritance by will, descent or survivorship, a parent giving a house to a child for token consideration, and a foreclosure deed handed to the lender (Wis. Stat. 77.25). Registered owners can also use the county's free Property Fraud Alert, which pings them when their exact name is listed on a newly recorded document as grantor or grantee. It is worth a look if you hold other property.

Within 10 days of signing the contract, you must give the buyer a completed Real Estate Condition Report if the property has one to four units. Hand it over late and the buyer may rescind during the next two business days and recover the deposit (Wis. Stat. 709.02). A personal representative, trustee or other fiduciary acting under a court who never lived in the house does not have to file it.

Before you fill it out, tour the house and jot down what you know about the basement, roof, plumbing and wiring. The form has a line for each known problem, and truthful answers protect you after closing.

Most Wisconsin property tax bills come due in two equal halves, on January 31 and July 31. Some municipalities adopt an ordinance for three or more payments, with half or more due by April 30 and the final balance by July 31 (Wis. Stat. 74.11 and 74.12). The next due date is January 31, 2027.

The City of Greenfield treasurer can report the unpaid balance, which the title company needs to split the bill between you and the buyer. Pay down what you can before picking a closing date.

Sketch the calendar before you sign. The contract date starts the clock on the condition report, so record it, and the work then splits into two parallel tracks.

The first track is paperwork: the report to the buyer, the payoff request to your lender, and title work. The second is the property itself, covering permits, any repairs you agreed to make, and the final walk-through. A cash buyer shortens the second track because there is no lender appraisal, though both tracks still end with a signed deed, the filed return and the recorded document.

Walk the buyer through any item you flagged in advance, so there are no surprises at the final walk-through. Hand over the house in the state you described on the form. Saved photographs and receipts are your best evidence if anyone raises a question later.

Where do heirs begin? Work out who has the legal authority to sign. A court-supervised fiduciary can sell yet is excused from the report for a home they never occupied. After that, collect the deed, the latest tax statement, and notes on keys, utilities and belongings left inside.

Estates often pair well with a cash purchase, as repairs, cleanouts and long showing periods fall away. Passing the house to an heir by will or descent owes no fee. The later sale to a buyer is a new transaction, run through title work, the return and the deed.

sections.h2: Fix it first or sell as is?
sections.html:
Repairing is your call. Defects you know of still go on the condition report, and an as-is buyer absorbs the work, saving some owners both cash and contractor hunting.

Price the large jobs, such as a roof or furnace, and set that cost against what a fixed-up house would fetch over an untouched one. If the gap is slim, cash gives a firm date without the wait for tours or loan approval. Heirs frequently decide that selling as is beats managing repairs on a vacant house.

faqs.q: Which county records a Greenfield, WI deed?
faqs.a: Milwaukee County, because Greenfield lies inside it. The Register of Deeds, at 901 N. 9th Street, Room 103, takes the filing and the transfer tax.

faqs.q: What is the transfer fee for a Greenfield sale?
faqs.a: It costs the seller 30 cents per $100 of value, rounding up any fraction. Inheritance by will or descent and a few family transfers are exempt under Wis. Stat. 77.25.

faqs.q: What should I check with the city before listing in Greenfield?
faqs.a: Ask the building inspection office about open permits, exterior orders, special assessments and tenant occupancy, then clear or disclose what you find.

faqs.q: Must I repair a Greenfield house before I sell?
faqs.a: No. Repairing is optional, but the condition report must disclose defects you know about, and an as-is buyer accepts the work.

faqs.q: When is Greenfield property tax due?
faqs.a: Twice a year, January 31 and July 31, unless an ordinance allows three or more payments. Your bill and the city treasurer give the exact amounts and dates.
